bio-oxygen-dissociation.title: The oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr shift
bio-oxygen-dissociation.caption: In the lungs haemoglobin is almost fully saturated. In respiring tissue, where pO₂ is low, the steep middle of the curve means a small fall in pO₂ releases a lot of oxygen. More CO₂ shifts the curve right (lower affinity), so even more is released; fetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left (higher affinity).
bio-oxygen-dissociation.alt: S-shaped oxygen dissociation curves of percentage saturation against partial pressure of oxygen, with the curve for high carbon dioxide shifted right and fetal haemoglobin shifted left.
description: The horizontal axis is the partial pressure of oxygen in kilopascals, from 0 to 14. The vertical axis is percentage saturation of haemoglobin, from 0 to 100.
The adult curve is S-shaped (sigmoid): flat at low partial pressure, steep in the middle, and levelling off near 97% at the partial pressure in the lungs (about 13 kPa).

The curve at high carbon dioxide (the Bohr effect) lies to the right of it: at the same partial pressure, haemoglobin is less saturated, so it has given up more oxygen. An arrow at 4 kPa shows the extra oxygen unloaded.
The fetal haemoglobin curve lies to the left: at the same partial pressure it is more saturated, so it can take oxygen from the mother's blood.

Shaded bands mark the partial pressures typical of respiring tissue and of the lungs. Curves are drawn from the Hill equation (n = 2.7) with P50 about 3.6 kPa for adult haemoglobin, 4.4 kPa at high CO₂ and 2.5 kPa for fetal haemoglobin: illustrative values, and real ones vary.

review.notes: Round 1: Bohr shift exaggerated (P50 4.8); now 4.4 kPa and labelled illustrative. Round 2: approve.

bus-supply-demand.title: Equilibrium, and what an increase in demand does
bus-supply-demand.caption: Equilibrium is where the curves cross: P = 20, Q = 60 for the worked example. Below it, at P = 15, buyers want 70 but sellers offer only 50: a shortage of 20 that pushes the price up. If demand increases (D → D₂), price and quantity both rise, to P = 25, Q = 70.
bus-supply-demand.alt: Supply and demand diagram with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal. Demand and supply cross at price 20, quantity 60. Demand shifting right moves equilibrium to price 25, quantity 70.
description: Price is on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, as is conventional in economics.
The demand curve D (Qd = 100 − 2P) slopes down; the supply curve S (Qs = 20 + 2P) slopes up. They cross at the equilibrium E: price 20, quantity 60.

At a price of 15, quantity demanded (70) is greater than quantity supplied (50): a shortage of 20, shown by a double-headed arrow between the two curves, which pushes the price up towards equilibrium.
A dashed curve D₂ (Qd = 120 − 2P) shows an increase in demand. It crosses supply at E₂: price 25, quantity 70. Both price and quantity have risen.

review.notes: Round 1: phone label clipped; surplus arrow crossed D₂; fixed by showing the shortage at P = 15. Round 2: approve.

chem-br2-bromonium.title: Adding Br₂ to cyclohexene: anti addition through a bromonium ion
chem-br2-bromonium.caption: The approaching π bond polarises Br₂. The π electrons bond to the near bromine, which uses a lone pair to bond to the other carbon, giving a bromonium ion that bridges the top face of the ring (wedges). The top face is blocked, so bromide attacks from the bottom face and that bromine ends up on a hash. The two bromines end up on opposite faces: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
chem-br2-bromonium.alt: Mechanism of bromine adding to cyclohexene: a bromonium ion forms on the top face, bromide opens it from the bottom face, giving trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.
description: Left: cyclohexene with a bromine molecule above its double bond, polarised δ+ on the near bromine and δ− on the far one. Three curly arrows: from the C=C bond to the near bromine; from a lone pair on that bromine back to the other double-bond carbon; and from the Br–Br bond to the far bromine.

Middle: the bromonium ion. A positively charged bromine bridges the two former double-bond carbons; both of its bonds are drawn as wedges, so it sits on the top face of the ring. A bromide ion approaches the right-hand carbon. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on bromide to that carbon, and another from that carbon's bond to the bridging bromine back onto the bromine.
Right: trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane. One bromine is on a wedge (top face) and the other on a hash (bottom face): the two bromines added to opposite faces, which is anti addition.

chem-hbr-propene.title: Adding HBr to propene
chem-hbr-propene.caption: Step 1: the π electrons attack the δ+ hydrogen and the H–Br bond breaks. chem-sn1-sn2-profiles.title: SN1 and SN2 energy profiles
chem-sn1-sn2-profiles.caption: SN2 has one transition state and no intermediate. SN1 has two transition states with a carbocation intermediate in the valley between them; the first barrier is the highest, so ionisation is the rate-determining step.
chem-sn1-sn2-profiles.alt: Two energy profiles. SN2: a single hump. SN1: two humps with a carbocation intermediate in the dip between them, the first hump higher.
description: Left panel, SN2: energy rises from the reactants to a single transition state, marked with a double dagger, then falls to the products, which are lower in energy than the reactants. The activation energy is marked from the reactants to the top of the hump.

Right panel, SN1: energy rises to a first, higher transition state (ionisation), falls into a shallow dip holding the carbocation intermediate, rises to a second, lower transition state (nucleophile attack), then falls to the products. The activation energy of step 1 is marked; it is the largest barrier, so step 1 is rate-determining.

review.notes: Round 1: labels on curves, no plateaus; fixed. Round 2: products label moved below the curve end.

chem-sn2-mechanism.title: SN2: hydroxide and (R)-2-bromobutane
chem-sn2-mechanism.caption: One concerted step, (R) → (S). The lone pair on hydroxide attacks carbon from the side opposite bromine while the C–Br bond breaks. In the transition state carbon is partly bonded to both, with the other three groups flat; they then flip over like an umbrella in the wind.

law-duty-of-care.title: Does a duty of care exist?
law-duty-of-care.caption: After Robinson, start with precedent rather than a three-stage test. Precedent can deny a duty as well as recognise one. Only a genuinely novel situation calls for incremental reasoning by analogy, with the Caparo factors weighed together. Separately, there is generally no duty to protect others from harm caused by third parties or to rescue, unless an exception applies.
law-duty-of-care.alt: Decision tree for whether a duty of care exists in negligence, following Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police, Caparo v Dickman and the omissions rule.
description: Question 1: is the claim that the defendant's own act made the claimant worse off, or, if it is about failing to protect them from harm, does an exception apply (the defendant created the danger, assumed responsibility, or had control of the third party or the source of danger)? If no, there is generally no duty: no general duty to prevent harm caused by third parties or to rescue (Smith v Littlewoods; N v Poole BC).

Question 2: is the situation genuinely novel, with no precedent deciding it? If no, follow the precedent: there is a duty where it recognises one (for example road users, doctor and patient), provided the kind of harm to this claimant was reasonably foreseeable; there is no duty where precedent excludes one (Robinson).

If the situation is novel: develop the law incrementally, by analogy with established categories, weighing reasonable foreseeability of damage, proximity, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty, together rather than as separate gates (Caparo; Robinson).

review.notes: Round 1: REJECTED (not novel ≠ duty exists; omissions branch a dead end; Caparo as sequential gates). Rebuilt to follow Robinson. Round 2: approve; the lesson's own K: line, which contradicted Robinson, was corrected.

maths-transformations.title: Tracking a maximum through two transformations
maths-transformations.caption: Track the key point. y = 3f(x − 1): inside the bracket moves x the opposite way (1 right), outside stretches y as written (× 3): (4, 6) → (5, 18). y = f(2x) − 5: inside halves x, outside moves down 5: (4, 6) → (2, 1).
maths-transformations.alt: Graph of a curve y = f(x) with a maximum at (4, 6), and its transformations y = 3f(x − 1), with maximum at (5, 18), and y = f(2x) − 5, with maximum at (2, 1).
description: Three downward parabolas on one set of axes. The original curve y = f(x) has its maximum at (4, 6).
y = 3f(x − 1) is the curve moved 1 to the right and stretched parallel to the y-axis by scale factor 3: it is three times as tall and its maximum is at (5, 18).
y = f(2x) − 5 is stretched parallel to the x-axis by scale factor ½ (so it is narrower) and translated 5 down: its maximum is at (2, 1).
Arrows run from (4, 6) to each new maximum.

phys-converging-lens.title: Ray diagrams for a converging lens
phys-converging-lens.caption: A lens with f = 10 cm. Use the ray rules: a ray parallel to the axis passes through F; a ray through the centre is undeviated; a ray through F emerges parallel. Where they meet is the image. At 2F the image is real, inverted and the same size; inside F the rays diverge and only appear to come from a virtual, upright, magnified image.

Object at 2F (20 cm away): the rays meet at 2F on the other side, forming a real, inverted image the same size as the object.

Object inside F (6 cm away): the rays spread out after the lens. Traced backwards (dashed), they meet 15 cm in front of the lens on the object's side, forming a virtual, upright image 2.5 times larger. This is a magnifying glass.

phys-fbd-slope.title: Box pushed up a rough slope by a horizontal force
phys-fbd-slope.caption: Four forces, each with a physical source. Weight acts from the centre of mass straight down; the normal force is perpendicular to the slope; friction acts down the slope, opposing the motion; the push P is horizontal. Because P presses the box into the slope, N is bigger than mg here: resolving perpendicular to the slope gives N = mg cos θ + P sin θ.
phys-fbd-slope.alt: Free-body diagram of a box on a slope at angle theta, with weight down, normal force perpendicular to the slope, friction down the slope and a horizontal push.
description: A right-angled slope rising to the right at angle theta, with a box resting on it.

Weight, mg, is drawn straight down from the box's centre of mass. The normal force, N, is drawn from the contact face, perpendicular to the slope, pointing away from it. Friction, f, is drawn along the contact face, pointing down the slope. The push, P, is a horizontal arrow arriving at the box from the left.

Because P is horizontal, part of it presses the box into the slope, so the normal force is bigger than mg cos theta: N = mg cos theta + P sin theta. With m = 2 kg, P = 15 N and theta = 25 degrees, N is about 24 N against a weight of about 20 N, and the arrows are drawn to that scale (friction's size is illustrative).

review.notes: Round 1: N drawn shorter than mg, an acceleration note with no arrow; fixed (arrows to scale for m = 2 kg, P = 15 N). Round 2: approve.

phys-kirchhoff-loop.title: Two opposing cells in one loop
phys-kirchhoff-loop.caption: Go round the loop: the 6 V cell is a rise, the 2 V cell (facing the other way) is a drop, and the resistance takes the rest. ΣEMF = ΣIR gives 6 − 2 = I × 4, so I = 1 A, driven by the 6 V cell. The 2 V cell has current forced through it backwards, so it is being charged.

Because the current flows into the 2 V cell's positive terminal, that cell is being charged.

chem-nitration.title: Nitration of benzene
chem-nitration.caption: π electrons from the delocalised ring attack the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, giving the arenium (Wheland) intermediate: the horseshoe shows the delocalisation broken at the sp³ carbon, with the positive charge spread over the other five, which is why this step is slow. HSO₄⁻ then removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, the C–H bonding pair restores the aromatic ring, and the catalyst H₂SO₄ is regenerated. The arrow from an N=O bond onto oxygen shows where nitrogen's extra bond comes from; A-level answers usually show only the ring-to-N arrow and write the product –NO₂.

chem-nucleophilic-addition.title: Nucleophilic addition: cyanide and ethanal

chem-sn1-mechanism.title: SN1: hydrolysis of 2-bromo-2-methylpropane
chem-sn1-mechanism.caption: Step 1 is slow: the C–Br bond breaks on its own, leaving a flat tertiary carbocation and bromide. Stage 2: the tertiary carbocation, a positive central carbon with three methyl groups in a flat arrangement, and a bromide ion. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on the oxygen of a water molecule to the positive carbon.

Stage 3: an oxonium ion, the central carbon bonded to an OH₂⁺ group. A curly arrow goes from a lone pair on a second water molecule to one hydrogen of the OH₂⁺ group, and another from that O–H bond onto the oxygen.
Stage 4: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a hydronium ion H₃O⁺ and a bromide ion.

chem-reaction-classes.title: Classifying an organic reaction
chem-reaction-classes.caption: Ask what happens to the starting molecule. Two molecules joining into one is addition; a group swapped for another is substitution; a small molecule lost to form a double bond is elimination. Oxidation, reduction, condensation and hydrolysis are named by what is gained or lost.
chem-reaction-classes.alt: A decision tree: does the number of molecules fall? If yes, addition. If no, is one group replaced by another? If yes, substitution; if no, is a small molecule removed to leave a multiple bond? If yes, elimination; otherwise a rearrangement.
description: First question: do two reactant molecules become one product? Yes means addition, as in ethene + HBr.
Otherwise: is one atom or group replaced by another? Yes means substitution, as in bromoethane + OH⁻.
Otherwise: is a small molecule such as H₂O or HBr removed, leaving a double bond? Yes means elimination; if not, the atoms have rearranged.

chem-born-haber-nacl.title: The Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride
chem-born-haber-nacl.caption: From the elements, sodium and chlorine are atomised (+107, +122), sodium is ionised (+496) and chlorine gains an electron (−349). The gaseous ions then form the lattice. Down −349 to Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g).
Down by the lattice enthalpy to NaCl(s), which is −411 below the start (the enthalpy of formation).
So the lattice enthalpy is −787 kJ mol⁻¹.

Emitted light has lower energy than absorbed light.

Wavy arrow: relaxation to the bottom of S₁.
Fluorescence: S₁ down to S₀.
Intersystem crossing: S₁ to T₁.
Phosphorescence: T₁ down to S₀, lowest energy.

phys-u01-decay-fluctuations.title: Ten nuclei against the exponential law
phys-u01-decay-fluctuations.caption: N = N₀e^{−λt} is exact for a huge sample: with 10²⁰ nuclei the relative fluctuations are only 1/√N ≈ 10⁻¹⁰. phys-u01-decay-fluctuations.alt: Graph of the fraction of nuclei remaining against time in half-lives: a smooth exponential curve halving every half-life, and a jagged step line for a sample of ten nuclei that drops one or two nuclei at a time.
description: The horizontal axis is time in half-lives, from 0 to 4; the vertical axis is the fraction of nuclei left, N/N₀.
The smooth curve is N/N₀ = e^{−λt}: 0.5 after one half-life, 0.25 after two, 0.125 after three.
The step line is one simulated sample of 10 nuclei. It drops by 0.1 each time a nucleus decays, at random moments, and strays visibly from the curve.
For large N the steps become too small to see and the sample follows the curve: the model is deterministic for large samples and probabilistic for single nuclei.

bio-action-potential.title: An action potential
bio-action-potential.caption: From a resting potential of about −70 mV, a stimulus that reaches the threshold (about −55 mV) opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels: depolarisation to about +40 mV. description: Resting: about −70 mV, inside negative.
A stimulus raises the potential to the threshold, about −55 mV.
Depolarisation: Na⁺ floods in and the potential rises to about +40 mV.
Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves.
Hyperpolarisation: the potential briefly falls below −70 mV.
The resting potential is restored.

bio-active-transport-gut.title: Pumping and co-transport in a gut lining cell
bio-active-transport-gut.caption: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to push 3 Na⁺ out into the blood for every 2 K⁺ it brings in, keeping sodium low inside the cell. Sodium then flows in from the gut through SGLT1 and drags glucose with it, against the glucose gradient: secondary active transport. Glucose leaves for the blood down its gradient through GLUT2.
bio-active-transport-gut.alt: A gut lining cell between the gut lumen above and the blood below. On the gut side, sodium ions and glucose enter together through a co-transporter. On the blood side, a sodium-potassium pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in using ATP, and glucose leaves through a carrier protein.
description: Gut side: Na⁺ flows in from 140 to 12 mmol per dm³, down its gradient, through the SGLT1 co-transporter.
Glucose enters through the same protein from 0.5 to 8 mmol per dm³, against its own gradient: the sodium gradient pays for it.
Blood side: the Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out (12 to 145) and 2 K⁺ in (4 to 140), both against their gradients.
Each cycle of the pump carries one more positive charge out than in, so the inside of the cell is left negative.
Glucose leaves for the blood (8 to 5) by facilitated diffusion through GLUT2.
Concentrations are illustrative: SGLT1 goes on absorbing glucose even when the gut holds less than the cell.

bio-animal-cell.title: An animal cell

bio-apoptosis-necrosis.title: Apoptosis or necrosis?
bio-apoptosis-necrosis.caption: Apoptosis is a controlled, energy-requiring suicide: the cell shrinks and breaks into apoptotic bodies that phagocytes remove quietly. Necrosis follows severe injury: the cell swells and bursts, and its contents leak out and cause inflammation.
bio-apoptosis-necrosis.alt: A flow chart: a controlled, energy-requiring death triggered by signals leads to apoptosis, with shrinking and no inflammation; death from severe injury leads to necrosis, with swelling, bursting and inflammation.
description: Is the death controlled and energy-requiring, triggered by a signal such as DNA damage or a death receptor? If so it is apoptosis: the cell shrinks, the DNA is cut up, apoptotic bodies form and phagocytes remove them without inflammation.
If the cause is severe injury (lack of oxygen, toxins, trauma) it is necrosis: the cell swells and its membrane ruptures, and its contents leak out and cause inflammation.

bio-calvin-cycle.title: The Calvin cycle: counting the carbon
bio-calvin-cycle.caption: Three turns fix three CO₂ (1 carbon each) onto three RuBP (5 carbons each), giving six GP (3 carbons each). One triose phosphate (3C) leaves for each three CO₂ fixed; six turns make one glucose (6C).

bio-cell-cycle.title: The cell cycle and its checkpoints
bio-cell-cycle.caption: Interphase (G₁, S and G₂) takes up most of the cycle, and M phase is mitosis and cytokinesis. The cycle can pause at three checkpoints, in G₁, G₂ and at metaphase, until problems are fixed. Cells that stop dividing leave for G₀.
bio-cell-cycle.alt: A cycle of four boxes, G1, S, G2 and M, with arrows between them labelled with the G1 and G2 checkpoints and the daughter cells that start the next G1.
description: G₁: the cell grows and carries out its normal functions; the G₁ checkpoint checks size, nutrients, growth signals and DNA damage before S phase.
S: DNA is replicated; DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C.
G₂: the cell makes proteins for division and the G₂ checkpoint checks the DNA has been copied correctly.
M: mitosis, with the spindle checkpoint at metaphase, then cytokinesis; two identical daughter cells return to 2C.
A typical cycle in cultured human cells takes about 24 hours.

S phase: DNA is replicated, so the content rises from 2C to 4C.
G₂ and M: 4C, each chromosome two sister chromatids.
Cytokinesis divides the DNA between two daughter cells, each back to 2C.

bio-growth-curve.title: The bacterial growth curve
bio-growth-curve.caption: Plotted as log₁₀ of the number of living cells, exponential growth is a straight line: with a 20-minute generation time the count doubles three times an hour (log₁₀ 2 = 0.301 per generation). A lag phase comes first, then the log phase, a stationary phase when growth equals death, and a death phase.
bio-growth-curve.alt: A curve of log of viable cell count against time in hours: flat for the first hour (lag), a straight rising line from 1 to 6 hours (log phase), flat from 6 to 10 hours (stationary) and falling afterwards (death).

Log phase: the count doubles every generation (20 minutes here), a straight line on a log scale: gradient 0.903 per hour.
Stationary phase: growth equals death as nutrients run out and wastes build up.
Death phase: more cells die than divide.
After n generations the population is the starting number × 2ⁿ: ten generations multiply it 1,024-fold.

description: p² (AA) falls from 1 to 0 as q rises.
2pq (Aa) peaks at 0.5 when q = 0.5.
q² (aa) rises from 0 to 1.
At every q the three frequencies add up to 1.

bio-lac-operon.title: When is the lac operon on?
bio-lac-operon.caption: Two questions predict the lac operon. Without lactose the repressor sits on the operator and the genes are off. With lactose the repressor is freed, but the operon is strongly expressed only when glucose is also absent, because then cAMP rises and the CAP protein helps RNA polymerase bind.
bio-lac-operon.alt: A flow chart: no lactose means the operon is off; lactose with glucose gives low expression; lactose without glucose gives high expression.
description: Is lactose present? If not, the repressor stays bound to the operator, blocking RNA polymerase: the genes are off.
If lactose is present, allolactose binds the repressor, which leaves the operator.
Is glucose also present? If so, cAMP is low, CAP is inactive and transcription is low.
If glucose is absent, cAMP binds CAP, which helps RNA polymerase bind the promoter: the operon is strongly expressed.

bio-limiting-factors.caption: At low light intensity the rate rises in proportion to the light, whatever the CO₂ concentration or temperature: light is the limiting factor. description: At low light intensity both curves rise together: light is limiting.

With more CO₂ the plateau is higher (100 against 50).
Glasshouses raise light, CO₂ and temperature to raise yields.

bio-mhc-pathways.title: Which MHC molecule presents the antigen?
bio-mhc-pathways.caption: Where the protein comes from decides the route. Proteins made inside any nucleated cell, including viral proteins, are cut up by the proteasome and shown on MHC class I to cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells. bio-prokaryotic-cell.title: A prokaryotic cell
bio-prokaryotic-cell.caption: A bacterium has no nucleus: its single circular chromosome lies in the nucleoid, free in the cytoplasm. Plasmids, 70S ribosomes, a wall, and often a capsule, pili and a flagellum complete the cell, typically 0.5–5 µm long.

Plasmids are small extra circles of DNA, often carrying genes such as antibiotic resistance.
70S ribosomes are scattered through the cytoplasm.
Pili on the surface attach the cell and transfer DNA; the flagellum turns to move it.
There is no nucleus, and no mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum or Golgi apparatus.

bio-protein-levels.title: Four levels of protein structure

Tertiary structure: the 3D fold of one chain: hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions between R groups.
Quaternary structure: two or more chains together, as in haemoglobin (four subunits).
Not every protein has a quaternary structure: only those made of more than one chain.

bio-reproductive-barriers.title: Where is the barrier?
bio-reproductive-barriers.caption: Reproductive barriers act in order. Prezygotic barriers stop fertilisation: the groups never meet or breed together, do not accept each other, or their gametes cannot fuse. Postzygotic barriers act after a zygote forms: the hybrid does not survive, is sterile, or its offspring are weak.
bio-reproductive-barriers.alt: A flow chart of questions from meeting and mating to hybrid fertility, each 'no' leading to a barrier: habitat or temporal, behavioural or mechanical, gametic, hybrid inviability, hybrid sterility or hybrid breakdown.
description: Do the groups meet in the same habitat and breed at the same time? If not: habitat or temporal isolation.
Do they accept each other as mates and fit together? If not: behavioural or mechanical isolation.
Can their sperm and eggs fuse? If not: gametic isolation.
Does the hybrid zygote develop and survive? If not: hybrid inviability.
Is the hybrid fertile? If not: hybrid sterility, as with mules.
Are later hybrid generations fertile and fit? If not: hybrid breakdown. If they are, there is no reproductive barrier.

bio-resistance-selection.caption: Antibiotics do not cause resistance; they select for it. Resistant cells survive: and divide with less competition.
A resistant population: resistance genes may also pass to other bacteria by horizontal transfer.

Overproduction: more offspring are born than can survive.
Differential survival: individuals with advantageous traits leave more offspring.
Allele frequencies change: advantageous alleles become more common.

bio-water-pathway.title: The path of water through a plant
bio-water-pathway.caption: Water enters the root hairs by osmosis and crosses the cortex by the apoplast and symplast pathways. At the endodermis the Casparian strip forces it into the symplast. In the xylem, transpiration creates tension and cohesion between water molecules pulls a continuous column upwards, until water leaves the leaf as vapour.
bio-water-pathway.alt: Six boxes in order: root hair, root cortex, endodermis, xylem, leaf and air.
description: Root hair: water enters by osmosis down a water potential gradient.
Root cortex: apoplast (walls) and symplast (cytoplasm).
Endodermis: the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast: water enters the symplast.
Xylem: water rises in a continuous column by cohesion and tension.
Leaf: water evaporates from the mesophyll walls.
Air: water vapour leaves through the stomata: transpiration.

bio-which-route.title: How does it cross the membrane?
bio-which-route.caption: Three questions about the cargo choose its route. Size first: particles and macromolecules go in vesicles. Then the gradient: anything moved against it needs a pump and ATP. Finally the chemistry: small non-polar molecules slip through the lipid, while ions and polar molecules need a protein.
bio-which-route.alt: A flow chart of questions leading to bulk transport, active transport, simple diffusion, osmosis or facilitated diffusion.
description: Is it a single small molecule or ion, not a macromolecule or particle? If not, it is moved in vesicles by endocytosis or exocytosis, using ATP.
Is it moving down its concentration gradient? If not, a pump moves it by active transport, using ATP.
Is it charged or polar? If not (oxygen, carbon dioxide, steroids), it crosses by simple diffusion through the lipid.
Is it a solute such as an ion, glucose or an amino acid? Then it crosses by facilitated diffusion through a channel or carrier protein.
If it is water itself, it crosses by osmosis, much of it through aquaporins.

phys-u07-g-inside-outside.title: g inside and outside a uniform Earth
phys-u07-g-inside-outside.caption: Gauss's law for gravity: inside a uniform sphere only the mass within r pulls, so g rises in a straight line from 0 at the centre to 9.8 m s⁻² at the surface (g = g₀r/R). Outside it falls as 1/r². At r = R/2 the field is half the surface value, 4.90 m s⁻².
phys-u07-g-inside-outside.alt: Graph of g against r/R: a straight line from zero at the centre up to 9.8 metres per second squared at the surface, then a curve falling as one over r squared. The point at half the radius is marked at 4.90.
description: The horizontal axis is distance from the centre in Earth radii (r/R); the vertical axis is g in m s⁻².
Inside (r < R) the enclosed mass grows as r³ and the surface area as r², so g = g₀(r/R): a straight line from 0 to 9.8.
Outside (r > R) all the mass counts as if at the centre, so g = g₀(R/r)²: 9.8 at r = R, 2.45 at r = 2R.
The example's point: at r = R/2, g = 4.90 m s⁻², half the surface value.

bio-choosing-a-test.title: Choosing a statistical test
bio-choosing-a-test.caption: Match the test to the data and the question. Counts in categories compared with expected counts: chi-squared. An association between two measured variables: correlation. Comparing group means: a t-test for two normally distributed groups, ANOVA for three or more, and Mann–Whitney U for two groups that are not normally distributed.
bio-choosing-a-test.alt: A flow chart from the kind of data and question to chi-squared, correlation, ANOVA, the Mann-Whitney U test or the t-test.
description: Are the data measurements rather than counts in categories? If not, compare the observed and expected counts with a chi-squared test.
Are you comparing groups? If not, you are testing for an association between two variables: correlation (Pearson or Spearman).
Are there exactly two groups? If not, compare three or more means with ANOVA.
Are the data normally distributed? If so, use a t-test; if not, the Mann–Whitney U test.

bio-chromatin-marks.caption: Histone acetylation loosens chromatin, which usually activates genes: the promoter is open to RNA polymerase. DNA methylation (methyl groups on cytosine, often near a promoter) and some histone methylation usually silence genes: the chromatin is tight and RNA polymerase cannot reach the promoter. These marks can be reversed and are copied when cells divide.

description: Histone acetylation loosens chromatin and usually activates genes.
DNA methylation, often near promoters, usually silences genes.
Deacetylation and some methylation tighten chromatin, silencing genes.
Marks can be reversed, so drugs that block DNA methyltransferases or histone deacetylases are used in some cancers.

bio-cloning-steps.title: Making recombinant DNA
bio-cloning-steps.caption: The gene is isolated and inserted into a vector cut with the same enzyme, ligase joins them, host cells are transformed, and the few cells that took up the plasmid are picked out by a marker gene such as antibiotic resistance. Select the transformed cells: marker gene: only they grow on the antibiotic.

bio-double-circulation.title: The double circulation
bio-double-circulation.caption: Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit. The pulmonary circuit takes oxygen-poor blood from the right heart to the lungs and back to the left heart; the systemic circuit takes oxygen-rich blood from the left heart to the body tissues and back to the right heart. Keeping the two circuits apart lets the systemic circuit run at high pressure without damaging the delicate lungs.
bio-double-circulation.alt: A loop of eight boxes: right heart, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left heart, aorta, body tissues and vena cava, with the oxygen-poor boxes in blue, the oxygen-rich ones in red and the lungs and body tissues, where gases are exchanged, in green.
description: Pulmonary circulation: right heart to lungs and back to the left heart.

Blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit.
Blue boxes carry oxygen-poor blood and red boxes oxygen-rich blood; the lungs and the body tissues are where the exchange happens.

bio-energy-pyramid.title: A pyramid of energy
bio-energy-pyramid.caption: Energy is lost at every step of a food chain as heat from respiration, uneaten parts, faeces and excretion, so typically only about 10% passes to the next trophic level. Secondary consumers: 100. Tertiary consumers: 10.

Energy is never recycled: it leaves the ecosystem as heat.

bio-gene-flow.title: Gene flow makes populations more alike

bio-gut.title: The path of food through the gut
bio-gut.caption: Food passes from the mouth along the oesophagus to the stomach, the small intestine, the large intestine and the rectum. Most digestion and absorption of nutrients happens in the small intestine.

Large intestine: absorbs water and forms faeces; the rectum stores them.
Accessory organs (liver, gall bladder, pancreas): food does not pass through them.

bio-logistic-growth.title: Exponential and logistic growth
bio-logistic-growth.caption: With unlimited resources a population grows exponentially, a J-shaped curve. In a real environment growth slows as the population nears the carrying capacity K, giving an S-shaped logistic curve. Growth is fastest when the population is K/2.

Logistic growth: slows as resources run short and levels off at the carrying capacity K = 1,000.
The logistic curve rises fastest when the population is K/2 = 500, at about 9 time units.
Carrying capacity is the maximum population the environment can support.

bio-nitrogen-cycle.title: The nitrogen cycle
bio-nitrogen-cycle.caption: Most organisms cannot use N₂ because its triple bond is so strong. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn it into ammonium; nitrifying bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate (by way of nitrite); plants assimilate nitrate into protein and DNA; decomposers return nitrogen from dead matter as ammonium; and denitrifying bacteria turn nitrate back into N₂ in waterlogged soil.
bio-nitrogen-cycle.alt: A ring of six nitrogen stores: atmospheric nitrogen, ammonium, nitrate, plants, animals and dead matter, joined by arrows for nitrogen fixation, nitrification, assimilation, feeding, death and excretion, ammonification and denitrification.
description: Nitrogen fixation: bacteria (Rhizobium, Azotobacter) or lightning turn N₂ into ammonia, which forms ammonium.
Nitrification: Nitrosomonas turns ammonium into nitrite and Nitrobacter turns nitrite into nitrate.
Assimilation: plants absorb nitrate to make proteins and DNA; animals get nitrogen by feeding.
Death and excretion pass nitrogen to dead matter; ammonification by decomposers turns it back into ammonium.
Denitrification: anaerobic bacteria turn nitrate back into N₂.

bio-pcr-cycle.title: One cycle of the polymerase chain reaction
bio-pcr-cycle.caption: Each cycle heats to separate the strands (about 95 °C), cools so primers can bind to each end of the target (50–65 °C), and warms to 72 °C so heat-stable Taq polymerase can extend them. Each cycle roughly doubles the target, so copies = initial number × 2ⁿ.

Annealing, about 50–65 °C: primers bind to each end of the target.
Extension, about 72 °C: Taq polymerase adds nucleotides from the primers.
The cycle repeats 25–35 times, doubling the target each time.

bio-root-section.title: A root in cross-section
bio-root-section.caption: From the outside in: the epidermis (some cells make root hairs), the cortex, the endodermis with its Casparian strip, and the vascular cylinder. bio-sanger.title: Sanger sequencing: chain termination
bio-sanger.caption: DNA polymerase copies the template, but a little ddNTP, which has no 3′–OH, is mixed in: whenever one is added, the chain stops. bio-sanger.alt: Ten fragments of a new DNA strand, one of every length from 1 to 10 bases, each ending in a coloured base; reading the last bases from shortest to longest gives GATTACAGCT.
description: The template is copied by DNA polymerase from a primer, using normal dNTPs and a little labelled ddNTP.
Whenever a ddNTP is added the chain stops, so fragments of every length are made.
Fragments are separated by size by capillary electrophoresis, and a laser reads the dye of each last base.
From the shortest fragment upwards the last bases read GATTACAGCT.
The template strand is the complement: CTAATGTCGA.

bio-water-hbond.title: Water molecules and hydrogen bonds
bio-water-hbond.caption: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder than hydrogen, so each water molecule is polar: δ− on the oxygen, δ+ on each hydrogen, with the hydrogens 104.5° apart. A δ+ hydrogen is attracted to the oxygen of a neighbouring molecule: a hydrogen bond, longer (0.177 nm) than the covalent O–H bond (0.096 nm) and much weaker (5–30 kJ per mole, against about 350 for C–C). A molecule can donate two and accept two, so up to four.

description: A water molecule is bent: H–O–H 104.5°.
Oxygen is δ− and the hydrogens are δ+: the molecule is polar.
A hydrogen bond links a δ+ hydrogen to the oxygen of another molecule, in line with the O–H bond.
O–H covalent bond 0.096 nm; hydrogen bond 0.177 nm.
The central molecule donates two hydrogen bonds and accepts two: four in all.
Each is weak (5–30 kJ per mole) but together they give water its cohesion, high boiling point and solvent properties.

bio-complement-cascade.title: The complement cascade
bio-complement-cascade.caption: Complement proteins circulate inactive and are activated in a cascade by three pathways: the classical pathway by antibodies bound to antigen, the lectin pathway by lectins binding sugars on microbes, and the alternative pathway directly on microbial surfaces. All converge on cleavage of C3. C3b coats pathogens (opsonisation) so that phagocytes eat them; C3a and C5a attract and activate immune cells (inflammation); and C5b with C6, C7, C8 and many C9 forms the membrane attack complex, a pore that lyses the pathogen. Host cells carry regulatory proteins that block complement on their own surfaces.

C3b leads to opsonisation and to C5. C5 leads to inflammation as C5a and to lysis as C5b joined with C6 to C9.

bio-dna-repair.title: DNA repair: which pathway for which damage
bio-dna-repair.caption: Proofreading corrects errors as DNA polymerase works. After replication, mismatch repair corrects mismatched bases that were missed; base excision repair removes single damaged bases such as oxidised ones; nucleotide excision repair removes bulky damage such as the thymine dimers that UV light causes; double-strand breaks are repaired by homologous recombination, which uses a sister chromatid as a template, or by non-homologous end joining, which can lose bases. The right-hand panel works through nucleotide excision repair on a short sequence: the gap is refilled using the other strand as the template, so the original sequence is restored.
bio-dna-repair.alt: Left: four boxes of damage, each with an arrow to its repair pathway. Right: four steps of nucleotide excision repair on a twelve-base sequence: a thymine dimer joins two adjacent Ts, a section containing it is cut out, the gap is refilled using the opposite strand as the template, and ligase seals the strand with the original sequence restored.
description: Mismatch repair corrects mismatched bases missed by proofreading.
Base excision repair removes single damaged bases, such as oxidised bases.
Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky damage, such as thymine dimers caused by UV light.
Double-strand breaks: homologous recombination (sister chromatid as the template) or non-homologous end joining (can lose bases).
Steps of nucleotide excision repair: detect the distortion, cut out a section of the damaged strand, DNA polymerase fills the gap using the other strand, ligase seals it.

bio-elbow-joint.title: The elbow: a hinge joint and an antagonistic pair
bio-elbow-joint.caption: A synovial joint has cartilage on the bone ends, synovial fluid and a capsule; ligaments join bone to bone. Muscles are attached to bones by tendons and can only pull. At the elbow, a hinge joint, the biceps and triceps are an antagonistic pair: when the biceps contracts and the triceps relaxes the forearm is pulled up; to straighten the arm the triceps contracts and the biceps relaxes. The bones act as levers with the joint as the pivot.
bio-elbow-joint.alt: A side view of an arm bent at the elbow. The humerus is horizontal and the forearm points up to the right. A capsule round the joint holds synovial fluid, with cartilage on the bone ends and ligaments joining the bones. A thick, contracted biceps above is joined to the forearm by a tendon, and a thin, relaxed triceps below is joined by a tendon behind the elbow.
description: Synovial joint: cartilage, synovial fluid and a capsule; ligaments join bone to bone.
Tendons join muscle to bone.
Muscles can only pull, so they work in antagonistic pairs: one contracts while the other relaxes.
Bending the elbow: the biceps contracts and shortens, the triceps relaxes and lengthens, and the forearm is pulled up about the hinge joint.
Bones act as levers, with the joint as the pivot.

After n stages the length kept is (2/3)ⁿ, which tends to 0: the removed lengths sum to 1.

phys-u19-fibre-critical.title: A fibre core meeting its cladding
phys-u19-fibre-critical.caption: Core n = 1.48 against cladding n = 1.46 gives sin θ_c = 1.46/1.48, so θ_c = 80.6° from the normal. A ray meeting the boundary at 75° is below it and leaks into the cladding (bending to 78.3°); at 85° it is totally internally reflected. Only rays nearly parallel to the fibre axis are guided.
phys-u19-fibre-critical.alt: Two ray diagrams at a core–cladding boundary: a ray at 75° escapes into the cladding at 78.3°; a ray at 85° is totally internally reflected; the critical angle is 80.6°.
description: The critical angle is sin⁻¹(1.46/1.48) = 80.6° measured from the normal to the boundary.
A ray at 75° is less than 80.6°, so part of it refracts into the cladding, bending away from the normal to 78.3°.
A ray at 85° exceeds the critical angle: all the light is reflected back into the core.
Because the critical angle is so close to 90°, only rays travelling at less than about 9° to the axis are trapped.

phys-u19-glass-refraction.title: Light entering glass at 40°

phys-u19-missing-orders.title: Double slit with d = 3a: orders 3 and 6 are missing
phys-u19-missing-orders.caption: The double-slit fringes cos²(πd sin θ/λ) sit inside the single-slit envelope (sin β/β)². With d/a = 0.3 mm/0.1 mm = 3, the fringe maxima fall at a sin θ/λ = n/3, and the envelope is zero at a sin θ/λ = 1, 2, …: orders 3, 6, 9… coincide with single-slit minima and are missing.
phys-u19-missing-orders.alt: Graph of intensity against a sin θ over λ from minus 2.2 to 2.2: a central fringe pattern with rapid oscillations inside a sinc-squared envelope, which is zero at plus and minus 1 and 2, where the third and sixth order fringes would have been.
description: The horizontal axis is a sin θ/λ; the vertical axis is intensity relative to the central maximum.
The dashed curve is the single-slit envelope (sin β/β)², with zeros at a sin θ/λ = ±1, ±2.
The solid curve is the envelope times the double-slit fringes cos²(3πu), with u = a sin θ/λ. Its maxima are at u = n/3 (orders n = 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, …).
Orders 3 and 6 would fall at u = 1 and u = 2, exactly at the envelope's zeros, so those fringes are missing.

phys-u20-l2-vector.title: The l = 2 angular momentum with m = 2
phys-u20-l2-vector.caption: For l = 2 the length is |L| = √(l(l + 1))ħ = √6 ħ = 2.45ħ, but the largest component along z is only L_z = 2ħ. phys-u20-step-reflection.title: Reflection from a 3 eV potential step
phys-u20-step-reflection.caption: Above the step (E > V₀ = 3 eV) the wave still reflects partially: R = ((k₁ − k₂)/(k₁ + k₂))² with k ∝ √E and k₂ ∝ √(E − V₀). At E = 5 eV, k₁/k₂ = √(5/2) = 1.58 and R = 0.05, so 5% of the electrons bounce back; T = 1 − R = 0.95. R falls as E rises but never reaches zero, and at E = V₀ all are reflected.
phys-u20-step-reflection.alt: Graph of reflection and transmission probabilities against electron energy from 3 to 12 electronvolts for a 3 electronvolt step: reflection falls from 1 to 0.05 at 5 electronvolts and keeps falling; transmission rises correspondingly.
description: The horizontal axis is the electron energy E in eV, above the 3 eV step; the vertical axis is the probability.

At E = 5 eV, R = 0.05: about 5% reflected, 95% transmitted.
As E grows, R decreases towards zero but a classical particle would never be reflected: this is a wave effect.
